en: A sack full of flour on which chickens sat and it became moist from their droppings—one should sift the dough outward and the rest is permitted. (Beit Yosef in name of R' Eliezer of Garmiza)

He should take in his hand and afterward must sift all the remaining flour (Maharshal); and so is the custom. Flour in a sack that mice bit—its law is likewise: if before Passover one must sift the flour; if crumbs like dry dough crumbs remain on the sieve they are discarded and the flour may be retained until after Passover. If found thus on Passover it is forbidden for benefit and sifting does not help. If the sack rests in its place without shaking and the flour did not mix, he takes in his hand the bitten place and ties the sack there under the bite with some flour; the remainder may be retained by sifting; nevertheless it is forbidden to eat on Passover. All this only when it appears the mice ate some of the flour; but if they bit only the sack and there is doubt perhaps they ate nothing—even if found on Passover it may be retained and is forbidden to eat; even if found thus before Passover, lest there is chametz that dried and crumbles. (My teacher in Bach siman 453) But the Gaon Maharam of Lublin wrote in responsum siman 119 that they should take other guarded flour to make matzot for the first two nights, and flour from mouse bites they should make matzot and bake all those matzot before Passover by sifting the flour; and that sieve through which they sifted the flour—one need not be stringent and it is permitted for everything:

He chews. This is the meaning of melogma as written siman 442; and Rokeach wrote that even if he already chewed and placed on his wound before Passover he must destroy and remove them—end. And so explained above siman 442 that any melogma not spoiled before Passover requires destruction—not like Beit Hillel YD siman 255 who wrote that not chewing is only during Passover; but if it was already chametz it is permitted to leave on Passover on any remedy—end. In truth this is not so; and the main difficulty that forced this distinction is from what Rambam wrote that when not in the manner of enjoyment, such as melogma for a wound, one may heal from chametz on Passover—initially there is none, for there it is gentile chametz (and no Jewish responsibility on it; Magen Avraham wrote further a remedy that the Jew buy the flour for the gentile and make melogma on eve of holiday, and Pri Chadash doubts much, for it should only be like a gift where we require recognizable action that he does not wish to accept—and here the opposite). It discusses unlike Jewish chametz as Kesef Mishneh wrote and so Magen Avraham and in responsum Emunat Shmuel siman 27. All this for illness without danger; but with danger even through the Jew himself from his chametz it is also permitted, so Magen Avraham and responsum Emunat Shmuel there and above siman 465 seif 2. Chametz that passed Passover is permitted—Chafetz Chayim see there. (Melogma path even without danger; eating only where danger—Rashba) Pri Chadash wrote: I was asked about one with frequent headache who places a poultice of flour and water and other drugs on his temples to ease pain—whether permitted on Passover; he answered forbidden; and concludes there indeed with fruit juice it is fine—see there:
His wound. But to chew and swallow immediately is permitted for it does not leaven immediately. Magen Avraham:

For saliva. Even if she expectorated blood—and it is explained in seif (4) [5] that blood does not leaven—nevertheless it is impossible without saliva flecks; and this is specifically when sucking. Chafetz Chayim:

Nullified. This does not refer to nullification before Passover, for this was not in the category of nullification once it leavened afterward as siman 446; rather since he gave before his animal it was nullified and he renounced it from his mind; nevertheless it is good to give them little by little so they leave none. Chafetz Chayim see there:

Saliva. Bach wrote that Mordechai also forbids only when saliva is found; so in Shach; and he challenged the Rav here since Rokeach explained explicitly only when saliva is found (and Mahari Weil) that in unspecified one must burn all remainder—this is certainly extra stringency—end. Nevertheless it appears to me specifically in a horse and the like; but in a cow that has saliva from unspecified, certainly one must destroy from unspecified; therefore give before it little by little as written:

The wall. And likewise a wooden wall—Magen Avraham see there. Chafetz Chayim wrote: it appears specifically when sweating from itself or from fire heat; but if sweating from heat and steam of hot blood it is like water that makes fit for all—see there:

They forbid. Or Zarua wrote that the permitters' view is primary and Magen Avraham wrote the forbidders' view is primary; good to retain until after Passover—Chafetz Chayim. See Tur that wrote regarding dry meat sweating from water it was rinsed in—its sweat leavens; and above siman 453 s.k. 15 from law of animal sweat:
The moistened. And it implies the rest of the flour is permitted even on Passover; nevertheless afterward sift—Bach and Maharshal and Taz wrote this is mere stringency—see there:
Impossible. Such as when moistened in many places:

He should sift. The moistened place will be like dough and remain above. It appears if he need not eat from the flour on yom tov it is forbidden to sift on yom tov—see siman 507—rather sift through a gentile to destroy chametz; or give to gentile as gift before it stood mil measure—Magen Avraham. (See siman 446 and 459):

Sifting. But if he takes in hand all the moistened place it helps even if dried—Chafetz Chayim and so Taz; even during Passover he permits in such case—for only where entire sack or large part moistened then impossible to take moist place; but if possible to take moist place—it is permitted. Chafetz Chayim:

And mixes. Although flour in flour is called wet in wet and we do not say it reawakens—nevertheless crumbs are different for they do not mix well and reawaken as siman 467 seif 4; therefore forbidden to eat and permitted to retain. But if dried on Passover it is like chametz mixed on Passover—for while moist it did not mix, therefore mixed on Passover and forbidden to retain—Magen Avraham. Or Zarua wrote: where doubt whether moistened from fruit juice etc. or leavening things—lenient to eat on Passover even if dried from double doubt perhaps fruit juice, and if you say other things perhaps nothing mixed—see there. Bach wrote: mice bit sack and ate flour and dried—before Passover sift flour, discard crumbs on sieve, flour may be retained; if found thus on Passover all forbidden for benefit. If sack unmoved without shaking, take bitten place (with some flour), tie sack there, sift, may retain, nevertheless forbidden to eat on Passover—all when visible mouse ate flour; if bit only sack and doubt perhaps ate nothing—even found on Passover may retain, forbidden to eat, even before Passover lest chametz dried and crumbles—end. Maharam of Lublin siman 119 ruled on sack bitten by mice: if baked matzot before Passover from that flour—not forbidden to eat on Passover except first two nights take other guarded flour; flour sifted from that sieve—no stringency, permitted for all—end. Taz wrote even if water fell and dried, if he recognizes moist place take it and sift rest; certainly for mouse bites take around bitten place, sift rest and eat on Passover—end. Magen Avraham wrote: in mice be more stringent, these mice are wicked and go through whole sack and eat, especially in barrel—therefore Geonim were stringent—end. So Mabit for this reason. Chafetz Chayim agreed like Taz to tie bitten place and permit rest by sifting in every case—end. Only when no moisture visible at bite; but if any moisture at bite, attribute to common thing perhaps mice urinated on flour—etc.:

And milk. Likewise milk in brine even boiling and clear, and certainly congealed—Shach. And above siman 462 from law of fat; Magen Avraham wrote likewise bile does not leaven (it is only moisture and blood) and therefore permitted to make dough for healing; Pri Chadash wrote likewise milk water does not leaven. In Halakhot Ketanot part 2 siman 211 wrote sweat leavens—see there. See Shach. Chicken droppings do not leaven—Tur. Likewise wheat in animal dung—Rokeach. In human excrement Chafetz Chayim is stringent—see there. Plain that all Tur and Mechaber wrote here that leaven—if stood without occupation for leavening time, for through occupation it does not come to leaven:

462—one who gives—learn from 461:
But in it and already nullified—meaning if nullified before coming to prohibition; and since rabbinic matter we do not establish prohibition in such case:
And some are stringent. For unspecified they have saliva as chapter 20 of Shabbos 102b and above end of siman 324:
463—sack, etc.

And some forbid. He holds it comes from moisture in it and compares to saliva which is offspring of water and makes fit as above. Book Rashogah compares to human sweat that does not leaven as seif 5 and also does not make fit like sweat—thus not offspring of water unlike saliva and armpit sweat that make fit—there chapter 6 mishnah 5 and mishnah 7:
464—he should take in hand. As Yerushalmi brings Rosh chapter 21 seif 13: one of R' Pedai's cases—a sack of oil in wheat storehouse—asked R' Bun: go scrape beneath you:
And if impossible, etc. As chapter 21: remove its place:
And specifically, etc. Magen Avraham s.k. 8:

465—dew leavens. Yerushalmi chapter 3 end halacha 1: one said on herbs permitted, on gleanings forbidden; another switches—R' Chanania son of R' Hillel: even per one who permits on herbs, on gleanings from six hours onward dew damages them; although at four hours dew melts, moisture does not pass until heat of day. They also said Yerushalmi end Terumot halacha 2: R' Yochanan in name of Rashbi—if one says seven liquids, tell him dew and water are one kind and they counted two—see there and in verse 'and he wrung full bowl of water':
And likewise urine, etc. As chapter 6 of Machshirin mishnah 5—they are offspring of water:
But blood and milk. They are seven liquids not included in water like urine and the rest; Yerushalmi spoke only of dew as above; in milk they said chapter 21 Yoma 1, etc.:
And human sweat. Pesachim 39b: she spat on her dry meat—even sweat on her meat; Rashash there:
466—and bake immediately. For l'chatchila forbidden even moment as siman 459 seif 2:
And if doubtful. For it is d'oraisa doubt:
